name: Azure Data Explorer
summary: Microsoft’s managed analytics database for logs, telemetry and time series, known internally as Kusto and queried with KQL; it began as the back end of Azure Monitor’s Log Analytics and Application Insights.
intro: Azure Data Explorer (ADX) is a cluster of virtual machines that holds databases of strongly typed tables. Ingested rows are written as extents, immutable horizontal shards of a table that start small and are merged in the background until each holds millions of rows. Every extent is compressed and indexed on its own, including full-text indexes on string columns and indexes on JSON-like `dynamic` columns, so a search for a term can skip most of the data. Persistent data lives in Azure Blob Storage; nodes cache extents on local SSD and in RAM, still compressed, under a cache policy that keeps recent data hot. Queries are compiled just in time to machine code, keep intermediate data in memory, and see a snapshot of the extents that existed when they started. Queued ingestion batches data from Event Hubs, IoT Hub, Event Grid, Kafka or the SDKs; streaming ingestion first lands small writes in a row store so they are queryable at once.

You query with the Kusto Query Language (KQL), a pipeline of operators such as `where`, `summarize`, `join` and `render`, with built-in functions for time series, anomaly detection, forecasting and geospatial work; a subset of T-SQL also works. Update policies transform rows as they arrive, materialized views keep aggregates current, and continuous export writes to Azure Data Lake Storage. KQL is also the query language of Azure Monitor Logs, Application Insights, Microsoft Defender and the eventhouses of Microsoft Fabric Real-Time Intelligence. Clusters are billed per minute for the VMs plus an ADX markup per vCore; a developer tier has no SLA, and a free cluster with about 100 GB of uncompressed storage needs no Azure subscription.
strengths: Ingests millions of events per second and answers ad-hoc queries over terabytes to petabytes of logs and telemetry in seconds
Indexes free text and semi-structured JSON on ingestion, so log search and analytics run in one store
KQL’s pipeline style and its time-series, anomaly and forecasting functions suit exploratory troubleshooting; the same skills carry over to Azure Monitor, Defender and Fabric
Storage is separate from compute: follower clusters can read the same data, and only recent data needs to sit in the hot cache
limits: Azure only and proprietary; KQL is mostly used inside Microsoft products, so skills and queries don’t move easily to other databases
Extents are immutable: deletes and updates rewrite shards, and it is not a database for row-by-row changes
You size and pay for a running cluster, and the developer tier and free cluster have no SLA
Fabric eventhouses now offer KQL databases as SaaS on shared Fabric capacity, so new projects on Azure have two overlapping options

story: Kusto started inside Microsoft as a side project: a core team of four developers working on the Power BI service needed ad-hoc queries over Microsoft’s own telemetry stream, found nothing that fit, and built it. Other internal teams adopted it within months. It became the back end of Azure Log Analytics, Application Insights, Time Series Insights and Windows Defender Advanced Threat Protection, and by 2018 over 25,000 Microsoft employees used it regularly, with 200 PB of data available for query. Its largest internal table took about 200 billion records a day.

Microsoft announced a public preview as Azure Data Explorer at Ignite in September 2018, nearly five years after the project began, and made it generally available on 7 February 2019. Microsoft Fabric, announced in May 2023, added a real-time analytics workload; its eventhouses now hold KQL databases.

choices.why: Once written, an extent never changes, so nodes can cache it without coordinating, queries get snapshot isolation by listing extents, and compute can scale or fail over separately from storage.

choices.choice: Index text and JSON on ingestion, coarsely
choices.why: Telemetry is full of free text and semi-structured fields. Term indexes kept per block of about 1,000 records stay small and fast to build, yet let queries skip most data.

Sorting improves compression but costs a lot of CPU on free text, so ADX compresses with LZ4 by default and lets you set a row order only where queries need it, which keeps new data quickly available.
Exploring logs means narrowing down step by step, so KQL reads like a Unix pipeline: each operator takes a table and passes a table on.
